newsitem.title: UK: London gold fixes firmer but lacks confidence.
newsitem.headline: London gold fixes firmer but lacks confidence.

text.p: Physical demand and short covering raised gold prices on Monday morning, but dealers said the market outlook remained uncertain.
A weaker Australian dollar tempted some Australian miners to sell forward, locking in the higher prices, and this slowed any rally potential the market might have had in the Far East, dealers said.
Gold was fixed at $321.35 per ounce, compared with $319.50 on Friday, as it continued the climb from a recent low fix of $315.75, which was its lowest setting since December 11, 1985.
The bullion market plunged at the beginning of this month on news that the Australian central bank had sold 167 tonnes of gold from its reserves during the previous six months.
The move cleared out over 60 percent of its reserves, and shocked the gold industry as Australia is the world's third largest gold miner after South Africa and the U.S.

Mining share analysts said the plunge in the gold price meant more than half of western world gold producers were losing money. South African and Australian producers who had not sold forward to lock in the higher prices of last year and earlier this year would definitely be working at a loss, they added.
"We are seeing panic producer hedge sales on every rise," one dealer said, adding that those interventions were unlikely to stop while prices were languishing.
Physical interest was unlikely to pick up significantly until the market was down to $319-$317, a dealer said.

Traders expected the market to aim for $308.00 "some time soon" , according to one dealer, which would mean taking out support at $319, $317 and $315 and, more significantly, removing any need for the speculative hedge funds to consider covering their huge short positions.
"The professionals and intra-day traders may have to cover but there is no reason for the funds to cover if they see $308 as a good level to aim for," one dealer said.
Platinum and palladium were both firmer despite the arrival of the first 1997 shipment last week of Russian metal to Tokyo.
Platinum was indicated at $406.00/$409.00, up $3.50, and palladium was $4.50 firmer at $171.00/$174.00.
"Zurich (deliverable) ingot is still commanding a premium. The market is very tight," one dealer said.
Silver was slightly easier at $4.36/$4.38, down two cents.
